_help: Research Bytes #02. Every fact is from the paper (IEEE AIC 2024); the Best Paper award is from the publications list. The demo sentence is an illustration (the paper does not list its 28 sentences) and is labelled as an example on screen.

meta.title: Continuous Sign Language Recognition Using Leap Motion Sensor
meta.short: Reading sign language, sentence by sentence
meta.venue: IEEE AIC 2024 · 3rd World Conference on Applied Intelligence and Computing, Gwalior

scenes.say: Today's paper: continuous sign language recognition, using a Leap Motion sensor. It won Best Paper at IEEE A I C 2024.
scenes.cap: Today's paper: continuous sign language recognition, using a Leap Motion sensor. It won Best Paper at IEEE AIC 2024.

scenes.say: About seven percent of people worldwide have hearing loss, around sixty three million in India alone. Sign language connects them, but most people can't read it.
scenes.cap: About 7% of people worldwide have hearing loss, around 63 million in India alone. Sign language connects them, but most people can't read it.

scenes.say: Many recognition systems handle single, isolated words. But real signing flows, word after word, and that's where they struggle.
So the team used a Leap Motion sensor: two infrared cameras and three infrared LEDs, tracking both hands in 3D, at ninety frames a second.
From each frame, they keep just twelve points: ten fingertips and two palm centres, each as x, y and z. Then they normalise them, so different hand sizes don't matter.
These sequences feed an L S T M, a neural network with memory, in two layers. It first learned isolated signs, then was fine tuned on continuous signing, with transitions between the words.
scenes.cap: These sequences feed an LSTM, a neural network with memory, in two layers. It first learned isolated signs, then was fine-tuned on continuous signing, with transitions between the words.

scenes.say: So a flowing sequence becomes words, and the words become a sentence.
The dataset: forty two sign words, each recorded ten times, four hundred and twenty recordings in all, plus twenty eight sentences.
scenes.cap: The dataset: 42 sign words, each recorded 10 times, 420 recordings in all, plus 28 sentences.

scenes.say: The L S T M recognised words with ninety point three five percent accuracy, and full sentences with ninety eight point two one. A standard S V M managed eighty six and ninety.
scenes.cap: The LSTM recognised words with 90.35% accuracy, and full sentences with 98.21%. A standard SVM managed 86% and 90%.

scenes.say: Next steps: combine cameras and audio, cover more sign languages, and run it on phones and wearables.
This work is by Niteesh Kumar, Sanket Salvi, Rashad Ahmed, Yash Panjwani and Venkatesh B H.
